tables.how: Every payee with a line under the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing in the Controller's Citywide Nonprofit Spending table, fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2026, as retrieved on 12 November 2026: 91 organizations with a payment in those years (3 more are in the table with nothing paid). The column for that table adds to the case's figures: $158,857,930 in fiscal 2019 from 56 organizations and $518,334,466 in fiscal 2026 from 81, a rise of 226%. The years between add to $181,494,761 (2020), $274,351,643 (2021), $337,930,835 (2022), $361,090,416 (2023), $406,040,966 (2024), $489,430,335 (2025). 31 of the organizations paid in fiscal 2026 were not paid in fiscal 2019; they received $91,154,416 in fiscal 2026. Beside each figure is what the same department paid the same organization in the Controller's table of every payment (Vendor Payments (Vouchers)): $173,545,853 in fiscal 2019 and $526,998,722 in fiscal 2026. 4 organizations that the nonprofit table lists under other departments only received small payments from this department in the table of every payment; they are listed with nothing in the first column. 1 yearly payment is printed under one name in the nonprofit table and another in the table of every payment, tied by its contract number and amount; both rows are kept and the last column says so. In the table of every payment the department also paid 404 payees that the nonprofit table does not list, $27,817,581 in fiscal 2026 and $538,701,847 over the eight years; the two largest are Chicago Title Company ($187,574,025) and Stewart Title Guaranty Co ($91,270,238). They are not nonprofits in the Controller's table, are not part of the case's figure and are not listed. $3,680,784 of the fiscal 2026 figure was paid to the Regents of the University of California, which the nonprofit table marks “UCSF” and keeps among the nonprofits. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus the renames and spellings that a shared contract number confirms.
tables.limits: A payment is money the City sent, not money an organization kept or spent on itself: rent subsidies and aid that a provider pays on to landlords and households are in these figures. Much of the rise paid for hotel rooms and new housing opened during and after the pandemic, which cost more per person than shelter; a larger payment is not a worse result. Neither table says what any organization achieved with the money: the City's public data does not report results by contract or by provider. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table, which by its own description keeps contracted services only, leaves out a kind of payment; neither is wrong for that reason. The year printed on a payment can be later than the year the payment was issued.

tables.how: Every yearly total for San Francisco in the federal government's published point-in-time counts: the workbook of counts by community for 2007 to 2022, the federal report for San Francisco for 2023 to 2025, and the City's own report for the count of January 2026, which the federal government had not yet published when the files were retrieved. The case's series keeps 6 of the 20: 2015, 2017, 2019, 2022, 2024, 2026, the years from 2015 with a new count of both shelters and streets. In the other years from 2015 the federal total repeats the street figure of the count before, or (2021) covers shelters only. For the four years of the case's series from 2019, the last two columns give the homelessness department's payments to nonprofits in the fiscal year of the same number, from the first list, and that sum divided by the people counted: $19,771 (2019), $43,581 (2022), $48,785 (2024), $65,011 (2026).
tables.limits: A one-night count misses people and its method changes between years, so two counts are not exactly comparable. Thousands of people become homeless each year, so a flat count can hide many who left homelessness. Dollars per person counted divides a year of payments by one night's count; it is not what was spent on any person, and the payments also house people who are no longer counted as homeless because they are housed. The share of people counted who were in shelter and not on the street rose over these years, which the City counts as progress. The fiscal year runs from July to June, so the January count falls in the middle of it.

tables.how: Every project line for San Francisco in the federal government's yearly project-level housing inventory files, 2019 to 2025, that is an emergency shelter, transitional housing or a safe haven and is open (current or new that year): 459 rows. Their year-round beds add to the published total of each year: 3,403 (2019), 3,530 (2020), 2,267 (2021), 2,606 (2022), 3,856 (2023), 4,370 (2024), 4,837 (2025). Left out, as the published totals leave them out: 27 lines for projects still under development (1,835 beds) and 61 lines with overflow or seasonal beds only, among them the lines filed under the name “FEMA NCS” in 2021 and 2022 (2,205 and 1,436 overflow beds). In 2019 the lines name 28 organizations and in 2025 34. The column of City payees gives the payee whose name matched the inventory's name when the files were downloaded, by the exact name or the name without punctuation and company suffixes; a match on the first words only is marked not confirmed.
tables.limits: The inventory names the organization that the local agency reported as running a project on the night of the count; some lines name a City department. It spells one organization in several ways from year to year, and the spellings are left as printed. The link from an inventory name to a City payee is by name only. Beds are places, not results: a line says nothing about how well a site was run, and the people counted there on one night can be more than the year-round beds where overflow beds were open. Projects that serve people fleeing violence are named in the federal file without an address, and no address is given here for any site.

tables.how: Every monthly value of the scorecard measure of households who move in to permanent supportive housing, from 2017-07 to 2026-09: 111 months. The case adds the twelve months of each fiscal year (July to June): 1,176 (2018), 1,009 (2019), 985 (2020), 906 (2021), 1,726 (2022), 2,068 (2023), 1,996 (2024), 1,825 (2025), 1,684 (2026). Its figures are 1,009 for fiscal 2019 and 1,684 for fiscal 2026, a rise of 67%. Fiscal 2027 has 3 months so far (380) and is not in the case.
tables.limits: The scorecard's own definition of the measure says: “Data deduplicated within a month; not deduplicated across the fiscal year so do not sum data.” A household counted in two months of one year would be counted twice in the case's yearly sums; a move-in normally happens once, so the sums are a close reading and not the City's own yearly figure. The measure leaves out rapid rehousing and other programs, and it counts move-ins, not how long a household stayed housed. It is a citywide figure: the City publishes no move-ins by provider, so no organization can be set beside it.

tables.how: The federal government's System Performance Measures for San Francisco and the ten communities the case compares it with, federal fiscal 2015 to 2024. The federal file calls each community a “CoC”, a Continuum of Care: the local body that plans homelessness services for an area. Listed are the people leaving emergency shelter, transitional housing, safe havens and rapid rehousing, those of them who went to permanent housing, the share (the second divided by the first), and the people entering homelessness for the first time. San Francisco's share in 2024 is 17.4% (891 of 5,131), the lowest of the eleven; the ten peers are Los Angeles City & County CoC 29.6%; Metropolitan Denver CoC 29.9%; San Diego City and County CoC 31.3%; Sacramento City & County CoC 32.8%; Portland, Gresham/Multnomah County CoC 33.8%; New York City CoC 37.7%; San Jose/Santa Clara City & County CoC 39.0%; Oakland, Berkeley/Alameda County CoC 39.5%; Houston, Pasadena, Conroe/Harris, Ft. Bend, Montgomery, Counties CoC 47.6%; Seattle/King County CoC 49.2%, with a median of 35.8%. San Francisco's highest share was 63.3% in 2018 (750 of 1,185). Its people homeless for the first time were 3,396 in 2015 and 6,639 in 2024; the figure for 2019, the first year of the case's money series, is 629.
tables.limits: The share fell mostly because the number of people recorded as leaving rose, from 1,185 in 2018 to 5,131 in 2024, while the number who went to permanent housing went from 750 to 891. The measure depends on how completely each community records where people go: a community that adds many shelter beds, or records more people leaving to an unknown place, shows a lower share without housing fewer people. San Francisco's own figures swing widely from year to year, which points to changes in what was recorded as much as in what happened. The federal fiscal year runs from October to September. The measure is for a whole community's system and cannot be divided among providers.
